name: TPS61040DBVR
title: Low-power PFM boost converter, outputs to 28 V, SOT-23 and WSON
summary: TPS61040 and TPS61041 are small step-up converters that run from 1.8 V to 6 V and make adjustable outputs up to 28 V, aimed at LCD bias rails and white-LED backlights. An internal 30 V N-channel switch is driven under pulse-frequency modulation with a fixed peak current, 400 mA (TPS61040) or 250 mA (TPS61041), switching at up to 1 MHz. Quiescent current is 28 µA typ, shutdown current 0.1 µA typ, and soft start, undervoltage lockout and thermal shutdown are built in. An external inductor, Schottky diode and feedback divider complete the converter.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: The basic boost: L1 charges from the input while the internal switch holds SW low, then discharges through Schottky D1 into CO when the switch opens. R1 and R2 divide the output down to FB, setting it anywhere from VIN to 28 V, with CFF across R1. EN is tied to VIN so the converter is always on. CIN decouples the input.

parts.note: upper divider resistor; value set by the output-voltage equation

circuits.title: LCD bias supply, 18 V (Figure 7-1)
circuits.description: An 18 V, 10 mA bias rail from 1.8 V to 6 V. L1 and D1 form the boost stage round the internal switch; R1 2.2 MΩ over R2 160 kΩ sets 18 V against the 1.233 V reference, and CFF 22 pF across R1 gives the error comparator the overdrive for single clean switching pulses. EN is tied to VIN. C1 is the input reservoir, C2 the output capacitor.

circuits.title: LCD bias supply with adjustable output voltage (Figure 7-5)
circuits.description: The 18 V LCD bias supply with a DAC or analog control voltage fed into the FB node through R3. A control voltage of 0 V gives 25 V out; 1.233 V gives 18 V. The rest of the circuit is the 18 V bias supply: L1, D1, R1 2.2 MΩ, R2 160 kΩ, CFF 22 pF, C1 and C2.

parts.value: DAC or analog voltage: 0 V gives 25 V, 1.233 V gives 18 V

circuits.title: LCD bias supply with load disconnect (Figure 7-6)
circuits.description: The 18 V, 10 mA bias supply with a BC857C PNP, Q1, between the rectifier and the load: emitter on the D1 and C2 node, collector on VOUT, base pulled to VIN through R3 200 kΩ. In shutdown it cuts the path from input to load. The divider R1 2.2 MΩ / R2 160 kΩ and CFF 22 pF sense the output after Q1. C3 0.1 µF on VOUT is optional.

circuits.title: Positive and negative output LCD bias supply (Figure 7-7)
circuits.description: A +10 V, 15 mA rail and a -10 V, 15 µA rail from 2.7 V to 5 V. The boost stage L1 6.8 µH, D1 and C2 makes V1, set by R1 1.5 MΩ over R2 210 kΩ with CFF 22 pF across R1. C3 1 µF couples the switch node to a diode pump, D2 to ground and D3 into C4, which forms the negative rail V2.

parts.note: listed as EMK316BJ105KF with C2 and C3

notes: C4 is marked 4.7 µF, while the parts list gives the 1 µF EMK316BJ105KF for C2, C3 and C4.

circuits.title: 3.3 V to 12 V supply (Figure 7-8)
circuits.description: A 12 V, 35 mA output from a 3.3 V rail. L1 6.8 µH and D1 make the boost; R1 1.8 MΩ over R2 205 kΩ sets 12 V and CFF 4.7 pF sits across R1. C1 10 µF on the input, C2 4.7 µF on the output, EN tied to VIN.

circuits.title: Two battery cells to 5 V (Figure 7-9)
circuits.description: A 5 V, 45 mA output from two cells, 1.8 V to 4 V. L1 3.3 µH and D1 boost; R1 620 kΩ over R2 200 kΩ sets 5 V with CFF 3.3 pF across R1. Efficiency is about 84 % at VIN = 2.4 V and 5 V / 45 mA out.
notes: Rated both 5 V / 50 mA and 5 V / 45 mA; the 84 % efficiency figure is at 5 V / 45 mA.

circuits.title: White LED supply, PWM brightness on EN (Figure 7-10)
circuits.description: Drives four white LEDs in series. The string runs from the boosted output to FB, with RS 82 Ω from FB to ground. A 100 Hz to 500 Hz PWM signal on EN sets brightness. The 24 V zener D2 across the output is optional. Efficiency is about 86 % at VIN = 3 V, ILED = 15 mA.

circuits.title: White LED supply, analog brightness on FB (Figure 7-11)
circuits.description: Four white LEDs in series with sense resistor RS 110 Ω; R1 120 kΩ joins the sense node to FB, and R2 160 kΩ brings an analog brightness control voltage onto FB: 3.3 V turns the LEDs off, 0 V gives ILED = 20 mA. EN is tied to VCC. D2, a 24 V zener across the output, is optional. A smaller C2 gives more LED ripple.

parts.value: analog brightness control: 3.3 V LEDs off, 0 V ILED = 20 mA

notes: L1 is marked 10 µH and D1 MBRM120L on the schematic, while the parts list gives Murata LQH4C3R3M04 (3.3 µH) and MBR0530.

operation.text: TPS61040 and TPS61041 differ in switch current limit: 400 mA typ for TPS61040 and 250 mA typ for TPS61041. The lower limit lets a smaller inductor with a lower current rating be used and gives less output ripple, for lower-power designs. TPS61040 comes in SOT-23 (DBV), SOT-23-THIN (DDC) and 2 mm × 2 mm WSON (DRV); TPS61041 in DBV and DRV. Automotive versions are TPS61040-Q1 and TPS61041-Q1.

The converter uses pulse-frequency modulation with a fixed peak current. When FB drops below the 1.233 V reference, the switch turns on and the inductor current ramps up. It turns off when the current reaches the set peak (400 mA or 250 mA typ), or after the maximum on time of 6 µs typ. The rectifier then carries the inductor current to the output, and the switch stays off for at least 400 ns typ and until FB is below the reference again. The converter therefore runs in discontinuous conduction with a frequency that follows the load, up to 1 MHz. The loop is inherently stable, so inductor and output capacitor can be chosen over a wide range.
About 100 ns typ passes between the current reaching ILIM and the switch opening, so the real peak overshoots the dc limit by VIN / L × 100 ns: more at high input voltage and with small inductors.
To limit inrush at start-up, the current limit starts at ILIM/4 for 256 switching cycles, rises to ILIM/2 for the next 256 cycles, and then goes to the full ILIM.

EN low shuts the device down, to 1 µA typ supply current. EN has to be terminated, not left floating. In shutdown the inductor and Schottky diode still connect input to output, so the output sits at the input voltage; a small external transistor can disconnect the load (load-disconnect circuit).
Below about 1.5 V typ input the main switch is held off.
The MOSFETs turn off above a junction temperature of 168 °C typ, with 25 °C typ hysteresis. These figures are statistical and not tested in production.

Inside: an undervoltage lockout and bias supply from VIN; an error comparator comparing FB with VREF = 1.233 V; an RS latch set through a 400 ns minimum off-time block and reset by the current-limit comparator or a 6 µs maximum on-time block; a gate driver for the N-channel power MOSFET between SW and GND, with RSENSE in its source; and soft start acting on the current limit. EN controls the device.

Since the loop is stable for any inductor, L mainly sets the switching frequency. Values from 2.2 µH to 47 µH suit; the largest usable value is set by the 6 µs typical maximum on time, within which the current must reach the peak limit. Choose L so the maximum switching frequency at full load is not exceeded. Smaller L gives higher frequency but lower efficiency; its effect on maximum load current is secondary. The inductor's saturation current must cover the peak current computed with the maximum ILIM, and lower dc resistance gives higher efficiency.
For battery-powered designs a high-impedance divider is used: R2 typically up to 200 kΩ and R1 at most 2.2 MΩ. Lower values make FB less sensitive to noise.

CFF across R1 gives the error comparator enough overdrive. Without it, or with too small a value, the switch fires double pulses or bursts instead of single pulses, raising output ripple; if that ripple is acceptable CFF can be omitted. Lower switching frequency needs a larger CFF. A larger CFF worsens line regulation.

Line regulation depends on the ripple at FB; about 50 mV peak to peak works well. Leaving out CFF gives the best line regulation but bursts raise output ripple, which a larger output capacitor reduces. With CFF fitted, FB ripple at or above 50 mV worsens line regulation; it can be improved with a smaller inductor (higher frequency, lower ripple) or with a small capacitor from FB to ground, starting at the same value as CFF, to bring FB ripple back to 50 mV.
A low-ESR output capacitor gives the best filtering. Ceramic types have low ESR; tantalum also works in some designs.
Low-ESR ceramic input capacitors are recommended; 4.7 µF suffices for most designs, more for better input filtering.
A Schottky diode is needed for high efficiency. Its current rating must cover the peak current computed with the maximum ILIM.
The input supply covers 1.8 V to 6 V and must be rated for the current that the input voltage, output voltage and output current call for.

Place the input capacitor as close to VIN as possible, and the inductor and diode as close to SW as possible, to keep switching noise out of nearby circuits. FB and its divider are high impedance: route them away from the inductor and shield them with ground plane or a ground trace. Make the power connections wide, and use a star ground or a ground plane to hold down ground shifts and noise.

In the SOT-23 example VIN, VOUT and GND are copper areas. The inductor runs from a small SW island at pin 1 to the VIN area, and the diode from the SW island to the VOUT area. The output capacitor bridges VOUT and GND; the input capacitor bridges VIN and GND beside pins 5 and 4. GND (pin 2) joins the ground area. The divider resistors and the feedforward capacitor sit below FB (pin 3), between the VOUT area and the ground strip.
